bib.title: Pattern Recognition and Machine Learning, Appendix C. Properties of Matrices (pp. 695-701)

question: Which matrix identities (inverses, trace, determinant, derivatives, eigendecomposition) does the book rely on?

results.claim: Woodbury identity: (A + B D^-1 C)^-1 = A^-1 - A^-1 B (D + C A^-1 B)^-1 C A^-1; cheap when A is large and diagonal and B has few columns.
results.quote:
which is known as the Woodbury identity and which can be veriﬁed by multiplying
both sides by (A + BD−1C).

results.claim: Identity C.5 (P^-1 + B^T R^-1 B)^-1 B^T R^-1 = P B^T (B P B^T + R)^-1: the right side is much cheaper when M << N (B is MxN).
results.quote:
Then if M ≪N, it will be much cheaper to evaluate the right-hand side of
(C.5) than the left-hand side.

results.claim: d/dx A^-1 = -A^-1 (dA/dx) A^-1 and d/dx ln|A| = Tr(A^-1 dA/dx).
Derivative of Tr(A B A^T) wrt A is A(B + B^T); d ln|A| / dA = (A^-1)^T.
A real symmetric matrix has real eigenvalues and orthonormal eigenvectors; A = U Lambda U^T, A^-1 = U Lambda^-1 U^T, |A| = product of eigenvalues, Tr(A) = sum of eigenvalues.
Positive definite is not the same as all elements positive: [[1,2],[3,4]] has eigenvalues 5.37 and -0.37.
results.note: The example matrix is not symmetric, so it illustrates only that positivity of entries does not give positive definiteness (eigenvalues of a nonsymmetric matrix are what is given).

limits: Not a tutorial; proofs mostly omitted; assumes inverses exist and dimensions conform.
Proof of C.22 is deferred ('prove later') and finally left as an exercise.
practices: Use the right-hand side of C.5 or the Woodbury identity (C.7) when it replaces inversion of a large matrix by inversion of a small one (pp. 696).
Check positive definiteness through eigenvalues, not through the sign of elements (p. 701).

terms.definition: Maximum number of linearly independent rows (or columns); equals the number of nonzero eigenvalues
Sum of the elements on the leading diagonal
A matrix with U^T U = I; its columns are orthonormal eigenvectors
A matrix with w^T A w > 0 for all w, equivalent to all eigenvalues > 0
